## Depth: Communicating Across Levels

One of the goals of designing with data is to avoid or diminish the necessity of "gut" decision making. Consequently, it can break hierarchical decision-making structures. The stereotype of management-led, top-down decision making based on hunches cannot flourish in a data-literate environment. Rather, company-wide data literacy that includes addressing well-formulated, carefully investigated questions, invites discussion, challenge, and most importantly the potential to be wrong.

This data is best when collected using any number of techniques (not just A/B testing, but also ethnographic field research, field deployments of prototypes, surveys, lab studies, usability research, etc.). Such grounded and carefully gathered user data can drive your decisions, and is a less risky prospect than relying on hunches from individual executives working from a "gut feeling." An early paper that focused on A/B testing published in 2007 by Ron Kohavi, Randal Henne, and Dan Sommerfield entitled "Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HIPPO," addressed this issue:

The underlying principle in this quotation from Ronny Kohavi is how data is an effective way to resolve conflicts in decision making without relying on rank, hierarchy, or company politics. John Ciancutti also shared some thoughts with us about how data can resolve conflicts in decision making within a company. He worked at Netflix for a number of years, eventually as VP of Product Engineering, and illustrates how data literacy across all roles at Netflix became a source of freedom and innovation within the company. He said:

Within the tech industry, Netflix has a reputation for being particularly effective at leveraging data. Throughout this chapter, we share a number of stories from Patty McCord who for over 12 years was the Chief Talent Officer at Netflix, where she oversaw talent acquisition and HR. She currently runs her own consulting business and has a great way of showing how an environment that embraces data can help its employees. Patty points out how having a mechanism to measure whether you are doing the right thing for your customers allows for more people to have a voice in the development of the product.

One of the things that made the data-driven approach so successful at Netflix was that the practice of leveraging data was well established and universally accepted throughout the company. It may have started at the top with Reed Hastings and Neil Hunt (Netflix CEO and CPO) driving and believing in the value of leveraging data, but it was also embraced by everyone through management to the individual contributors on the team.

While at some companies the CEO might get to do whatever he wants, at Netflix Patty says it's different:

Patty highlights a common tendency, that any employee, including executives, can get caught up in thinking they know the answer. One of the reasons that embracing A/B testing can help to mitigate a top-down approach to problem solving is that everyone can learn from experimentation. For example, when Reed would engage in product testing and had a strong idea for what he wanted to see in the product, he would submit his ideas to the same rigor of A/B testing as everyone else in the product team. On rare occasions, Reed might dictate the exact way that a product idea would work, but he would do this on "his test cell"; that is, on the experimental group in the test that he was backing. This cell would be tested against other cells that were proposed by the product team. If it didn't win, then it didn't get launched. Having the upper-level management hold themselves accountable to the same process as the individual teams therefore reinforced the practice of subjecting ideas, prototypes, features, and flows to grounded review through experimentation, and to the possibility of "failing" as a positive outcome. This value was central to a view of how the company should work.

If you are trying to shift into a data-aware framework, it will be critical to look at the way product and design decisions have been made to date. If these decisions were largely in the hands of one or two individuals, then it's worth taking the time to make sure that those people can understand and recognize the value of bringing in user/customer data into the decision-making process because in the end, they may find that their weight is diminished (as is the "weight" of any individual opinion). This is a good point to check with yourself as well — are you also comfortable and willing to see how incorporating data will change the weight of your own opinion within the design and product development process?

## Mechanisms for Distributing Decision Authority

The mechanism by which data literacy redistributes decision authority operates through systematic experimentation rather than advocacy. When A/B tests serve as the arbiter of which ideas proceed, the evaluative criteria shift from political influence or seniority to measurable impact on user behavior. This creates a neutral referee that neither rewards nor penalizes the source of a hypothesis. At Netflix, this mechanism extended beyond product decisions to shape cultural norms: the expectation that all ideas—including those from executives—must pass through experimental validation became embedded in how work got done. The test cell concept provided a specific implementation: even when Reed Hastings had strong convictions, his proposed solution competed in the same experimental framework as team-generated alternatives. The outcome was determined by results rather than by organizational rank.

## Conceptual Distinctions

The chapter draws a sharp distinction between opinion-based and evidence-based decision frameworks. Opinion-based decisions weight the source of the idea; evidence-based decisions weight the evidence itself. This distinction matters because it reframes what constitutes a valid contribution to product development. In an opinion-based system, seniority and persuasiveness influence outcomes; in an evidence-based system, the quality of the experimental design and the clarity of the measured outcomes determine success. The chapter also distinguishes between individual data literacy (one person understanding data) and organizational data literacy (data-driven norms pervading company culture). Netflix's success stemmed from the latter: data literacy was not a skill held by specialists but a shared operating assumption across all levels.

## Caveats and Limitations

The chapter acknowledges that shifting to a data-aware framework requires careful attention to existing power dynamics. When decisions have historically been made by one or two individuals, those people may resist an approach that diminishes their influence. The chapter suggests that this transition requires those individuals to recognize the value of user data—not to be compelled to abandon their judgment entirely, but to accept that their opinions now carry less weight than evidence when the two conflict. A further caveat applies to the types of questions data can answer: well-formulated, carefully investigated questions are prerequisites for useful data, meaning that data literacy includes not just statistical competence but also question-framing skills. Not all decisions can be resolved through experimentation; some require judgment where data provides context but not answers.

## The Netflix Test Cell Example

The test cell mechanism at Netflix illustrates how organizational commitment to data-driven decision making was operationalized in practice. When Reed Hastings had a strong product conviction, he could designate one experimental cell as his own proposal. This cell would run alongside alternative proposals from the product team, all subject to identical experimental conditions. The outcome was determined by which cell performed better on the defined metrics. If Reed's cell lost, the feature did not launch regardless of his position. This approach meant that executive ideas received no special treatment in evaluation—though they did receive the benefit of being tested rather than assumed correct. The practice reinforced that failing an experiment was not a personal failure but a normal outcome of the process, and that learning what doesn't work has value.

# Appendix C: Statistical Methods Used in Our Research

**Measurement Validation.** The research employs confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), per Brown (2006), to validate that survey items properly load onto their intended latent constructs. CFA tests hypothesized measurement models rather than discovering structure post-hoc. The authors apply psychometric theory (Nunnally, 1978) to establish construct reliability via Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability, and assess convergent and discriminant validity through average variance extracted and Fornell-Larcker criteria. Straub et al. (2004) guides validation decisions consistent with positivist research norms.

**Structural Modeling.** Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) estimates relationships between technical and organizational practices and outcomes. Chin (2010) and Gefen and Straub (2005) provide reporting standards; Chin et al. (2003) addresses interaction effect estimation via Monte Carlo simulation. PLS maximizes explained variance in dependent constructs and handles smaller samples and non-normal data better than covariance-based SEM. Hair et al. (2006) covers multivariate techniques including regression and factor analysis underlying PLS.

**Common Method Variance.** The authors address bias from self-reported surveys using Lindell and Whitney's (2001) marker variable technique, which statistically isolates method variance from true construct relationships.

**Survey Design.** Dillman (1978) informs instrument construction to reduce response errors and improve data quality.

**Conceptual Distinctions.** CFA differs from exploratory factor analysis by testing a priori structure. PLS differs from covariance-based SEM by prioritizing predictive relevance over exact model reproduction, enabling flexible estimation with complex organizational data.

**Caveats.** Statistical remedies address only part of common method variance; procedural controls during survey design provide additional but incomplete mitigation. PLS has lower statistical power than covariance-based approaches for equivalent sample sizes.

## Retirement Announcement

BA proposed retiring in October (end of summer schedule); Air France chose May—reflecting divergent post-crash attitudes. Unable to coordinate, each airline announced independently.

## Forum 150

The retirement was announced at an extraordinary Forum 150 meeting on 9th April 2003, switched to the 10th to avoid the 34th anniversary of first flight. Bannister delivered the news in uniform, encountering the "Marmite factor"—roughly two-thirds expressed sadness, the remainder relief.

## The Mantra

At the press conference, Bannister coined: "It's the right decision at the right time for the right reasons"—immediately adopted as the party line.

## Branson Offer

BA's response to Branson's offer was that government funding meant the transfer decision wasn't theirs—a cop-out containing enough truth. A senior Virgin pilot privately confided they'd have gone bust.

## One Aircraft Retained

Concorde required a Certificate of Airworthiness and Type Certificate, unlike the Vulcan's simpler "Permit to Fly." Infrastructure cost of £60 million annually would rise £40 million regardless of fleet size. Airbus refused to transfer the Type Certificate—the air-intake computer technology remained proprietary and secret due to military applications.

## Public Celebration

Discussion shifted toward celebrating Concorde's legacy. Edward de Bono observed she appealed to both brain hemispheres—technologically superb and artistically graceful. Most Brits felt individual ownership: "That's my Concorde up there."

## Retirement Announcement and Public Response

The retirement-as-celebration concept gained traction, though BA and Air France couldn't coordinate timing—BA planned October (end of summer schedule), while Air France retired in May due to post-accident sentiment in France.

The announcement was scheduled for Forum 150 on 9th April 2003, the 34th anniversary of Concorde's first flight, but Bannister suggested switching to the 10th. He announced retirement to senior management in uniform, facing the "Marmite factor"—roughly two-thirds expressed sadness, the remainder relief.

The press mantra emerged during Q&A: "It's the right decision at the right time for the right reasons." Regarding Richard Branson's offer, BA's party line was that government funding meant transfer wasn't their decision—a cop-out containing enough truth.

On retaining one aircraft for air shows: unlike the Vulcan's "Permit to Fly," Concorde required the higher-standard Certificate of Airworthiness and Type Certificate. Infrastructure cost of £60 million per annum would soar by another £40 million, remaining constant regardless of fleet size. Airbus wouldn't transfer the Type Certificate—the air-intake computer technology was proprietary and secret due to military applications.

Public discussion shifted from retirement motives to celebrating Concorde's legacy. Edward de Bono observed she appealed to both brain hemispheres—technologically superb and artistically graceful. Bannister believed most Brits felt individual ownership: "That's my Concorde up there."

# How to Apply These Ideas to Business

The Four Laws of Behavior Change—Make It Obvious, Attractive, Easy, and Satisfying—apply to organizations and teams, not just individuals.

## Automation at Scale

Onetime actions can lock in good habits at scale. John Henry Patterson implemented cash registers to automate honesty and reduce theft, similar to how technology locks in good habits for individuals.

## Culture as Collective Habits

Organizations build culture the same way individuals build habits. The British Cycling team's "aggregation of marginal gains" approach demonstrates how tiny 1% improvements compound into organizational excellence.

## Practical Business Tools

Key habit-building tools translate to business contexts:

- **Habit stacking**: Creating routines where completing one task triggers the next (e.g., Patterson's daily ritual before selling)
- **Environment design**: Redesigning workspaces to make desired behaviors automatic
- **Accountability structures**: Seinfeld's "don't break the chain" method applies to teams
- **Reflection and review**: Decision journals and regular check-ins help organizations adapt systems

## Addition by Subtraction

Reducing friction applies to eliminating wasteful processes. Organizations improve by removing unnecessary steps and automating repetitive tasks, not just adding new initiatives.

## Application to Employees

Companies can help employees build good habits by making cues obvious, behaviors attractive, productive work frictionless, and quick wins satisfying.

# How to Apply These Ideas to Business

This chapter (page 265 in the printed edition) applies the Four Laws of Behavior Change to organizational and business contexts.

## Core Principles

The habits framework that works for individuals—Make It Obvious, Attractive, Easy, and Satisfying—applies equally to companies and teams. Business success depends on building systems of good habits at the organizational level.

## Automation at Scale

The same automation principles from individual habit formation scale to business operations. John Henry Patterson (predecessor to NCR) implemented a cash register system to automate honesty and reduce theft, similar to how technology can lock in good habits for individuals.

## Culture as Collective Habits

Just as individuals build identity through habits, organizations build culture. The British Cycling team's "aggregation of marginal gains" approach under Dave Brailsford demonstrates how tiny 1% improvements compound into organizational excellence.

## Practical Business Tools

Key habit-building tools translate to business contexts:

- **Habit stacking**: Creating routines where completing one task triggers the next (e.g., Patterson's "sharpening the saw" daily ritual before selling)
- **Environment design**: Redesigning workspaces to make desired behaviors automatic
- **Accountability structures**: Seinfeld's "don't break the chain" productivity method applies to teams and organizations
- **Reflection and review**: Decision journals and regular check-ins help organizations adapt and improve systems

## Addition by Subtraction

Reducing friction applies to eliminating wasteful processes. Organizations improve by removing unnecessary steps and automating repetitive tasks, not just adding new initiatives.

## Application to Employees

Companies can help employees build good habits by:

- Creating obvious cues through prompts and reminders
- Making desirable behaviors attractive through incentives
- Reducing friction for productive work
- Celebrating quick wins to make habits satisfying
